name: Under-eye chemical peel (TCA/lunch peel)

card.summary: A chemical peel aimed at the thin skin under the eyes to lighten pigment and smooth texture; popular in discussion, thinly studied for this exact site.
card.aka: TCA peel, lunch peel, periorbital peel
card.note: Periocular skin is thin; documented peel risks include pigment change, scarring and prolonged redness.

quick.overview:
An under-eye chemical peel applies an acid solution, such as trichloroacetic acid (TCA), to the lower-eyelid area to remove outer skin layers. People in appearance communities discuss it as a way to address darkness, fine lines and crepey texture under the eyes.

Peels in general are an established dermatology tool for texture and pigment. Published trials specific to peeling the under-eye area are not part of the material reviewed for this entry, so its evidence for dark circles is described here as limited.
quick.mechanism: Peel acids cause a controlled injury to the epidermis and sometimes upper dermis, after which the skin sheds and regenerates. Depth depends on the acid, its strength and how it is applied; TCA is classed as a medium-depth agent.
quick.risks: Reported peel complications include prolonged redness, pigment changes, skin thinning, texture changes, milia and scarring, with higher risk from deeper peels and unsupervised home kits. The skin around the eyes is thin, and peels are performed by clinicians in medical settings. No sources reviewed give a regulatory status specific to this use.

lead: An under-eye chemical peel applies an exfoliating acid, most often trichloroacetic acid (TCA), to the skin of the lower eyelids and infraorbital area. People use it to lighten dark circles caused by pigment, smooth crepey texture and soften fine lines, so the eyes look more rested and the midface looks fresher. "Lunch peel" is cosmetic-practice shorthand for a quick peel with limited downtime. [1]

Chemical peeling is a long-established cosmetic procedure in which an acid removes outer skin layers and prompts regrowth; light peels are done in clinics and med spas, while medium-depth peels such as TCA are performed by medical providers. [1] Periorbital hyperpigmentation, the condition most people mean by dark circles, is a common trait involving excess melanin, most prevalent between ages 16 and 25. [2]

Research specific to the under-eye area is small but real. A 2013 case series used a low-strength TCA and lactic acid combination weekly for four sessions in 30 patients and reported improvement in most, [3] and a randomised comparison of 62 patients found microneedling with 10% TCA improved pigment where CO2 laser alone did not. [4] A dermatology review notes that there are no randomised trials of peels alone for the condition. [5]

chain: Acid removes outer layers of thin lower-eyelid skin
Skin sheds and regenerates, with less pigment on the surface
angle.text: A peel lightens pigment-type dark circles and refines texture by controlled exfoliation of the lower eyelid skin, giving a brighter, more rested look. Clinicians usually describe a series of gentle sessions rather than one deep peel. [5][3]

infobox: Trichloroacetic acid, often in low strength or combined with lactic acid [3][5]
Four weekly sessions in one case series; every 2-4 weeks suggested in a review [3][5]
At least 4-6 months with sun protection in most patients in one series [3]

paras: Chemical peels are classified by depth. Alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic and lactic acid are the mildest; salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid used for acne; TCA is a medium-depth peel done in offices or outpatient surgical centers and commonly causes a warm or burning sensation; phenol-croton oil peels are the deepest. [1] Peeling is described as reducing fine lines, acne scars and uneven pigment through controlled injury. [1]

Periorbital skin is thin and has few follicles and sebaceous structures to support re-epithelialisation, so a review of dark-circle treatments says deep peels are not recommended there and recommends a staged approach of lighter peels with sessions every 2-4 weeks, stopping retinoids or hydroxy acids beforehand. [5] Published protocols for the area tend to use low acid strengths, such as 3.75% TCA with 15% lactic acid [3] or 10% TCA after microneedling. [4]

Dark circles have several causes, including pigment, visible blood vessels, shadowing from volume loss and thin skin. [2] Peels address the pigment and texture component. Practitioners and forum users describe the peel as most relevant when the darkness is brownish and flat rather than from hollowing.

Peels were introduced in the second half of the 19th century by Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra, who used agents including phenol and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities; phenol-croton oil peels entered mainstream practice in the 1960s. [1]

General peel complications include photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning, texture changes and scarring, especially with unsupervised home kits. [1] In the 2013 series, side effects were described as mild and temporary and included redness, swelling, frosting, dryness and visible small vessels (telangiectasias). [3] In the randomised comparison, transient redness lasting up to a week occurred in 58% of the microneedling-plus-TCA group. [4]
Because the skin is thin and adjacent to the eye, reviews caution against deep peels at this site. [5] Sun protection is described as important for maintaining results. [3]

A case series by Vavouli and colleagues (J Cosmet Dermatol, 2013) treated 30 patients with skin types II-IV using 3.75% TCA plus 15% lactic acid weekly for four sessions. Physicians rated 93.3% of patients as having fair, good or excellent improvement, patients rated 96.7% similarly, and benefit lasted at least 4-6 months in most who used sun protection. [3]

A randomised comparison of 62 patients with mild to moderate infraorbital dark circles, presented by Banu Farabi and colleagues at an American Academy of Dermatology meeting, gave three monthly sessions of either microneedling plus 10% TCA or CO2 laser. The combination showed significant improvement at day 90 (p = .012) maintained to day 180, while laser alone showed none at day 90. [4]

A review in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology states there are no randomised controlled studies of chemical peeling alone for periorbital hyperpigmentation and that support is largely anecdotal. [5] A separate registered phase 3 trial studied a medium-depth peel on lateral canthal wrinkles with or without botulinum toxin pretreatment, a different goal. [6]

Phenol-croton oil peel enters mainstream practice. [1]
